# 0013 — Hand-written ML in Go rather than a Python inference service

**Status:** Accepted. Every model in the tree is trained and validated on
**synthetic data generated by its own tests**. No model here has seen a real
retailer's transactions.

---

## Context

USSLP's pricing engine makes decisions at three tiers
(`platform/internal/pricing`):

- **Tier 1**, the rules engine: pure, deterministic, sub-millisecond. Every price
  the platform ever displays passes through it.
- **Tier 2**, edge ML: a per-store demand model and an expected-margin optimiser
  inside an **8–15 millisecond budget**.
- **Tier 3**, cloud optimisation: asynchronous, every fifteen minutes, ensembling
  a sequence model with trees and correcting for cross-elasticity between
  substitute SKUs.

Tier 2 is the constraint that decides everything. It has to run **on a Store
Gateway Unit** — a fanless x86 box in a stock room with 2 GB of RAM, no Python
runtime, no BLAS, and no reliable WAN — and it has to keep working when the cloud
is unreachable, which rules out calling a hosted model
([0003](0003-edge-first-architecture.md)).

Tier 1 has a related but stricter requirement: it must reach the *identical*
decision in the cloud service and in the gateway's offline brain, or
reconciliation after an outage rewrites prices customers have already seen.

## Decision

**Everything is plain Go over flat `float64` slices, in `platform/internal/pricing/ml`.**

| Model | File | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| Log-log elasticity regression | `elasticity.go` | Own-price elasticity with a confidence interval |
| Gradient-boosted regression trees | `gbt.go` | Demand prediction |
| Isolation forest | `isoforest.go` | Price and telemetry anomaly detection |
| LSTM | `lstm.go` | Sequence model for Tier 3 |
| int8 quantisation | `quantise.go` | The smallest gateway tier |
| Model serialisation | `serialize.go` | One-pass load on the gateway |

Tier 1's rules engine (`pricing/domain`) imports nothing but `canon` and the
standard library, contains no clocks, no I/O and no randomness, and allocates
nothing on the evaluation path beyond one small violation slice. Given the same
constraints and the same requested price it produces the same decision on every
tier, forever.

Three design choices inside the models are worth recording because they are where
the "hand-written" decision earns its keep rather than merely costing:

**Elasticity refuses to produce a number it cannot defend.** The `Elasticity`
struct does not expose a bare coefficient. It carries a standard error, a
confidence interval, an R², the observation count, the count of *distinct price
points*, a `Usable` flag and an operator-facing `Reason`. One price point means no
slope is identified at all however many observations there are, which is the
classic way a retail elasticity model produces a confident number from nothing.
The defaults are deliberately conservative: refusing to optimise a SKU costs a
price that stays where a human put it, while acting on a spurious elasticity is a
systematic margin error repeated across every store and discovered in a quarterly
review.

**Quantisation measures its own loss rather than bounding it theoretically.** A
`float64` tree node is 32 bytes; the quantised form is 6 — one int8 threshold, one
int8 leaf value, one int16 feature, one int16 child index. A 120-tree depth-5
per-store model goes from roughly 590 kB to 110 kB, and more importantly fits in
the gateway's L2 cache, which is where the latency win actually comes from. What
is lost is precision in two places, and `QuantisationDelta` measures both on
held-out data; the model registry refuses to promote a quantised model whose
measured delta exceeds the tenant's tolerance.

**Training failure is an error, not a degraded model.** `ErrTraining` exists
because a silently under-trained pricing model is worse than no model — the
platform will act on it.

## Consequences

**Tier 2 runs where it has to.** No Python, no serving container, no network call
on the decision path, and no dependency that has to be present on 100,000
appliances.

**Tier 1 is bit-identical across tiers by construction**, which is what makes
autonomous pricing during an outage safe to reconcile
([0009](0009-hybrid-logical-clocks-for-reconciliation.md)).

**The code owns its own correctness, and the tests are built for that.** Every
model is tested against synthetic data generated from a known ground truth, so
the assertions recover a parameter the test itself chose rather than asserting
that today's output equals yesterday's. That is a genuinely stronger test than a
regression fixture.

**And it is also the limitation.** The root `README.md` states it plainly and this
record repeats it: every model is trained and validated on synthetic data
generated by its own tests. The algorithms are tested against known-truth
generators. **No model here has seen a real retailer's transactions, and none of
the demand curves it produces should be quoted as a finding about retail.** What
has been demonstrated is that the implementations recover parameters correctly,
not that the models are useful.

**No autodiff, no optimiser ecosystem, no GPU.** Changing the LSTM's architecture
means writing the backward pass. That is a real tax on iteration speed for
whoever owns Tier 3, and Tier 3 is the tier with the least reason to be in Go —
it runs asynchronously in the cloud every fifteen minutes and has none of Tier
2's constraints.

**Numerical correctness is now the platform's problem.** `pricing/ml` has to get
its own gradient computations, its own splitting criteria and its own numerical
stability right, with no library to defer to. The tests are the only thing
standing between a subtly wrong optimiser and a systematic margin error.

**Model interpretability was chosen deliberately elsewhere too.** The mesh's
predictive self-healing model (`edge/sec/predict.go`) is a five-feature logistic
regression whose coefficients are documented as "a smooth version of extrapolate
the LQI trend three minutes forward and compare it with the reroute threshold,
adjusted by three secondary signals". Stating it that way rather than presenting
the weights as inscrutable is the difference between a model an operations team
can reason about at three in the morning and one they can only switch off.

## Alternatives considered

**A Python inference service (FastAPI, TorchServe, Triton).** The obvious answer,
and the right one for Tier 3 alone. Rejected because Tier 2's decision has to be
made on the gateway with the WAN down, and a hosted model is unreachable by
definition at exactly the moment a store most needs a price. Splitting Tier 2
between a Python service in the cloud and a Go reimplementation on the gateway
would mean two implementations of the same model, which is the failure mode
`firmware/src/crypto/usslp_canon.c` goes to some trouble to avoid on the
attestation path.

**ONNX Runtime with Go bindings.** Would have let the models be trained in Python
and executed in Go. Rejected on cgo — `CGO_ENABLED=0` is what makes the arm64
cross-compile for gateways trivial — and on binary size on an appliance.

**Gorgonia or another Go ML framework.** Rejected under
[0010](0010-go-and-hexagonal-architecture.md)'s no-dependency rule, and because
the models needed are small and well understood: a log-log regression, boosted
stumps, an isolation forest. The framework would carry far more than is used.

**Doing Tier 3 in Python and Tiers 1–2 in Go.** Defensible, and it is what a
production team would probably do. Not what was built, and the cost of not doing
it is the iteration tax noted above.
